column4: The stone's water "فَانفَجَرَتْ" joins the source section's bursting-water sense of f-j-r to an apportioned drink, since every people knows its drinking place; rupture and measured water meet in one scene.

God makes the earth burst into springs, "وَفَجَّرْنَا الْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا," and the waters meet according to a matter already measured; this gathers the section's rupture, earth, water, meeting, and measure.
Some stones have rivers burst from them and others split so water comes out; these two concrete openings preserve the water-breaking sense from which the section reads moral fujur.
The challengers demand that the Messenger make a spring "تُفَجِّرَ لَنَا مِنَ الْأَرْضِ"; it is a direct Quranic use of f-j-r for water breaking out of ground.
They demand a palm-and-grape garden with rivers made to gush through it abundantly; the root's bursting sense here produces the cultivated field developed in the section.
God's servants drink from a spring that they make gush abundantly, "يُفَجِّرُونَهَا تَفْجِيرًا"; the controlled opening contrasts with fujur as uncontrolled inward overflow.
When the seas "فُجِّرَتْ," a cosmic boundary bursts at judgment; this gives the section's water-breach sense its largest destructive scale.
The oath "وَالْفَجْرِ" places the dawn itself before the reader, the light-bearing rupture from which the source section begins its f-j-r meeting.
The night of decree remains peace "حَتَّىٰ مَطْلَعِ الْفَجْرِ"; dawn is the appointed boundary that ends a night, reinforcing the section's orderly turn rather than a lawless breach.

God is "فَالِقُ الْحَبِّ وَالنَّوَىٰ," the splitter of grain and date-stone; the same kind of opening that yields life from a field clarifies the source section's meeting of inward breach, dawn, and cultivation.
فَالِقُ الْإِصْبَاحِ makes dawn an opening, then places night, sun, and moon in a calculated order; it directly joins the section's torn darkness to the orderly cosmic watch.
The sun and moon move "بِحُسْبَانٍ," by calculation; this supplies the measured cosmic order that the section carries into the soul and its allotted consequences.
God raises the sky and sets the balance; the source section likewise makes the built sky the model for a soul set in order.
أَلَّا تَطْغَوْا فِي الْمِيزَانِ turns cosmic balance into a ban on transgression, exactly the section's move from ordered heavens to Thamud's tughyan.
The command to uphold weight justly and not diminish the balance illuminates the violated water-share and the exactly measured return described in the section.
The ayah explicitly opposes "الْمُتَّقِينَ" and "الْفُجَّارِ"; it is the clearest external pairing of the two inward portions named together in 91:8.
The righteous are in bliss, forming the positive half of the immediate two-outcome contrast whose fujjar half appears in 82:14.
وَإِنَّ الْفُجَّارَ لَفِي جَحِيمٍ gives fujur its opposed final field beside the righteous outcome in 82:13.

What people earn lays a rust "رَانَ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِم"; this is a pointed reversal of the section's imagery, because tearing the protective cover through fujur produces a corrupt covering over the heart.
Ordinary clothing covers nakedness, then "لِبَاسُ التَّقْوَىٰ" is named the better garment; this directly supports the source section's developed sense of taqwa as a protective covering.
Garments "تَقِيكُمُ الْحَرَّ" and armor "تَقِيكُم بَأْسَكُمْ" physically shield and restrain harm, preserving the concrete protective sense behind the section's taqwa image.
بَلْ يُرِيدُ الْإِنسَانُ لِيَفْجُرَ أَمَامَهُ presents fujur as a person's forward-projecting intention; it matches the section's inward tearing that releases a self-propelled transgression.

God "بَعَثَ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا" who recites and purifies them; this joins the section's contrast between a messenger whom God raises and the culprit who raises himself, while also meeting the soul's tazkiya.
Abraham asks God to "وَابْعَثْ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا" who will purify them; divine sending and cultivation of the soul stand together, unlike the self-dispatch of 91:12.
God is the one who "بَعَثَ فِي الْأُمِّيِّينَ رَسُولًا" who purifies them; it makes explicit both sides of the section's sent-messenger versus self-launched sinner meeting.
إِنَّا مُرْسِلُو النَّاقَةِ فِتْنَةً لَّهُمْ explicitly makes God the sender of the she-camel, sharpening the section's contrast with the man who sends himself toward her.
The water is "قِسْمَةٌ بَيْنَهُمْ" and every drink has its turn; it supplies the measured water-share that the source section says Thamud violated, while 54:29 supplies the attack.
They call their companion, and "فَتَعَاطَىٰ فَعَقَرَ"; this is the parallel scene in which one man undertakes the act and hamstrings the camel after the apportioned drink of 54:28.
لَهَا شِرْبٌ وَلَكُمْ شِرْبُ يَوْمٍ مَّعْلُومٍ states the camel's and people's measured turns at water, the exact quota whose breach the section connects to their own allotted return.

The wrongdoers have a "ذَنُوبًا" like their companions' portion; this Quranic share-word, with its bucket background identified by the source section, makes punishment an allotted draw related to ذنب.
فَكُلًّا أَخَذْنَا بِذَنبِهِ makes each community's destructive seizure follow its own sin, directly matching the section's rear/act/consequence meeting.
Thamud make palaces "مِن سُهُولِهَا" and carve mountain houses; this is the section's exact plain-and-palace scene before the inhabited ground is ruined.
Thamud are pictured amid "جَنَّاتٍ وَعُيُونٍ"; together with the crops, palms, and carved houses in 26:148-149, it supplies the flourishing field that their act will destroy.
وَزُرُوعٍ وَنَخْلٍ gives the crops and palms whose flourishing heads make the source section's barren-field and severed-palm senses of ʿaqr perceptible.
Their confident carving of mountain homes completes the cultivated-land scene of 26:147-148 and anticipates the leveling of the civilization built upon it.
The command to see "عَاقِبَةُ مَكْرِهِمْ" ends with God destroying the Thamud plotters and their people together; it is the exact aftermath the section locates behind the struck animal.
فَتِلْكَ بُيُوتُهُمْ خَاوِيَةً بِمَا ظَلَمُوا leaves their houses empty because of wrongdoing, concretely completing the destruction announced in 27:51.
After mentioning what is on earth, the ayah turns to heaven and "فَسَوَّاهُنَّ سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ"; it directly joins earth, built heavens, and creative taswiya as the source section does.
God "خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّاكَ فَعَدَلَكَ" creates, completes, and balances the human; it is the closest external formulation of the soul/body being fitted like the built sky.
God "سَوَّاهُ وَنَفَخَ فِيهِ مِن رُّوحِهِ" forms the human and breathes spirit into him, making the inward self the third constructed dwelling described by the section.
God announces that after He has fashioned the human, "سَوَّيْتُهُ," and breathed spirit into him, the angels must bow; taswiya here is bodily and inward completion.
The repeated Adam scene again joins divine taswiya with the breathing of spirit, reinforcing the section's constructive use of the root for the human self.
From a clinging form God creates and "فَسَوَّىٰ" the human; the embryonic context supplies another bodily sense of completion behind the section's fashioned soul.

A believer rebukes his companion for denying the One who created him from dust and a drop, then "سَوَّاكَ رَجُلًا"; human taswiya becomes a moral argument against the owner's corrupt use of his garden.
God is able "عَلَىٰ أَن نُّسَوِّيَ بَنَانَهُ" even to fashion fingertips at resurrection; constructive taswiya reaches the body's smallest detail and counters the flattening sense.

The barrier-builder fills the gap until "سَاوَىٰ بَيْنَ الصَّدَفَيْنِ," making the structure level with the two cliffs; this different root-sense shows leveling as deliberate construction rather than destruction.
God places sustenance in the earth and measures it in four days "سَوَاءً لِّلسَّائِلِينَ"; equal provision and measured earth illuminate the camel's apportioned water.
The warned parties will know who follows "الصِّرَاطِ السَّوِيِّ"; the root here marks the even or right road, clarifying the section's claim that Thamud chose the wrong way from a fitted order.
أَمِ السَّمَاءُ بَنَاهَا begins a creation sequence that parallels the section's built sky; 79:28 specifies its taswiya and 79:30 the spread earth.
God raises the sky's canopy and "فَسَوَّاهَا"; this is the direct constructive use of the same verb that the section sets against Thamud's leveling.
God darkens its night and brings out its morning brightness, restaging the orderly covering and opening at the start of surah 91.
وَالْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ دَحَاهَا supplies the spread earth that stands between the section's formed heavens and leveled people.
The spread earth yields its water and pasture, joining rain, ground, and growth within the same creation sequence.
The mountains are fixed in place; this continues the ordered earth scene of 79:30-31 and marks the stability opposite Thamud's ruined built landscape.
مَتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ makes earth's growth provision for people and livestock, including the animal-world dimension of the section's camel and pasture.
الَّذِي خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ makes taswiya the completion and fitting of creation, the constructive pole of the section's final word-meeting.
وَالَّذِي قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ places measure and guidance immediately after creative taswiya, clarifying why violated measure is also a wrong path in the section.
God "أَخْرَجَ الْمَرْعَىٰ," bringing out pasture after creation and measure; it supplies the living field attached to the section's spread land.
God then makes pasture dark stubble, "غُثَاءً أَحْوَىٰ"; this reversal from growth to waste illuminates the section's cultivated field turned barren.
A dead land is revived and grain is brought from it; it directly supplies the section's field as an image of what is cultivated rather than buried.
Gardens are planted and springs are made to burst, "وَفَجَّرْنَا فِيهَا مِنَ الْعُيُونِ"; f-j-r here creates the watered field rather than a moral flood.
People eat the fruit of the revived, irrigated ground; this states the provision produced by the bursting springs in 36:34.
Night is a sign from which God strips daylight, leaving darkness; the stripping image closely matches the section's reciprocal covering and uncovering.
The sun runs to its appointed station, expressing the exact placement and ordered movement with which the section opens.
The moon is measured through stages until it returns like an old palm stalk, joining measured succession with the palm-field imagery developed in the section.
Neither sun overtakes moon nor night precedes day; the cosmic boundary makes the section's contrast with the soul that breaks its limit especially clear.
Night covers day while pursuing it swiftly, and sun, moon, and stars remain subject to command; it restages the ordered cover-and-turn sequence carried into the soul.
God spreads earth, places stabilizers and paired fruits, then makes night cover day; this single ayah meets the section's spread ground, growth, and ordered covering.
God wraps night over day and day over night while sun and moon run to fixed terms; the reciprocal wrapping is the ordered succession that the final irreversible judgment ends.
God makes night and day "خِلْفَةً," successors to one another; this directly supports the source section's reading of the close as a final turn after which no counter-turn comes.
God makes the sun radiance, the moon light, and measures its stations so years and reckoning can be known; this is the calculable heavenly order carried into moral measure by the section.
The alternation of night and day and the creation of heavens and earth are signs; it joins the ordered watch of 10:5 to the whole built cosmos.
Night and day are two signs: the night sign is effaced and the day sign made visible so time can be counted; covering, opening, and calculation meet explicitly.
God creates night and day, sun and moon, each swimming in an orbit; the four actors of the surah's opening remain within one ordered motion.
The question of an unbroken night asks who besides God could bring light; by suspending alternation, it exposes how much the section's ordered watch depends on a divinely set boundary.
The matching question of an unbroken day asks who could bring night for rest; it is the converse boundary to 28:71 and clarifies the normal succession evoked by the section.
When God wills harm for a people, "فَلَا مَرَدَّ لَهُ"; this directly states the section's final claim that no later turn can repel the judgment.
The disobedient wish "لَوْ تُسَوَّىٰ بِهِمُ الْأَرْضُ"; taswiya here means being leveled with the ground, the destructive pole paired in the section with forming sky and soul.
After the mountains are scattered, God leaves the earth "قَاعًا صَفْصَفًا," a bare level plain; this is the physical result invoked by the section's destructive taswiya.
No crookedness or rise remains in that plain, completing the exact flattening scene of 20:106.
فَأَمَّا ثَمُودُ فَأُهْلِكُوا بِالطَّاغِيَةِ makes Thamud's destruction arrive through an overwhelming event named from the same transgressive field as their tughyan.
Thamud carve rock in the valley; the verse supplies the built landscape that the source section imagines returned to a flattened plain.
The peoples just named "طَغَوْا فِي الْبِلَادِ"; it explicitly connects Thamud's landscape to the transgression that upsets the section's measured order.
They multiply corruption in the lands, showing the outward spread of the inward fujur and tughyan described in the section.
God pours upon them a scourge of punishment; "فَصَبَّ" reverses the section's life-giving water into a measured destructive outpouring.
Salih presents "نَاقَةُ اللَّهِ لَكُمْ آيَةً," orders that she graze God's earth, and forbids harm; this is the full divine-camel commission behind the compressed scene in surah 91.
They hamstring the camel, defy their Lord's command, and demand the threatened punishment; the deed is explicitly both bodily attack and broken boundary.
The quake seizes them and leaves them fallen in their dwelling, completing the bodily and architectural consequence of 7:77.
Salih tells Thamud that God produced them from earth and settled them in it; this makes their built, cultivated land a divine trust before they ruin it.
Salih names God's camel as a sign, lets her feed in God's earth, and warns against harm; the verse joins messenger, animal, pasture, and approaching consequence.
After they hamstring her, their remaining enjoyment is measured as three days; the fixed term makes their own allotted aftermath answer the violated share.
The blast seizes the wrongdoers and leaves them fallen in their homes, realizing the section's image of people and dwellings struck together.
They become as though they had never flourished in those homes; this erasure turns an inhabited built place into the section's barren aftermath.
The people of al-Hijr carve mountain houses while feeling secure, restaging the durable architecture whose apparent order cannot shield transgression.
The blast takes them in the morning, placing judgment at a turn of night and day as the section's closing watch does.
What they had earned does not avail them; this gives the carved houses of 15:82 no power to reverse the morning judgment of 15:83.
Salih forbids obedience to "أَمْرَ الْمُسْرِفِينَ," those who exceed bounds; it identifies the social command opposite the messenger's restraining warning.
Those leaders corrupt the earth and do not set things right; the statement carries the section's inward breach into ruined land and order.
Salih forbids touching the camel with harm and warns of a tremendous day's punishment, binding the protected animal directly to consequence.
They hamstring her and become regretful; the physical cut immediately begins the moral aftermath developed by the section.
The punishment seizes them, completing the hamstringing scene and showing the consequence following the deed.
Nine men in the city corrupt the land and do not reform; this collective background makes the section's single self-launched wretch part of an organized breach.
They swear to attack Salih and his family by night, making night itself the cover for their transgression before their plan returns upon them.
They devise a plan and God devises while they do not perceive; the reversal prepares the irreversible outcome named in 27:51.
God saves those who believed and "كَانُوا يَتَّقُونَ" beside the ruined houses of 27:52; taqwa functions as the protection the transgressors tore away.
One blast leaves them like the dry crushed material of a pen, converting a living herd-and-field setting into flattened plant debris.
God spreads the earth, anchors it, and grows in it "مِن كُلِّ شَيْءٍ مَّوْزُونٍ"; spread ground, cultivation, and measure meet exactly as in the section.
Earth is made a bed, sky a structure, and rain produces fruits; this is the same heaven-earth house and cultivated provision that the section sets before the soul.
God makes earth a settlement and sky a structure, forms people well, and provides good things; built cosmos, human formation, and provision appear as one ordered home.
Earth is made a cradle with paths, and water from heaven brings out paired plants; this gathers spread ground, guidance, rain, and cultivated growth.
People eat and pasture their livestock from the plants of 20:53, completing the section's relation between field, provision, and animal.
Water is poured abundantly before the earth is split and grain grown; it begins the rain-to-field sequence implicit in the section's cultivated earth.
ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا الْأَرْضَ شَقًّا makes the field's rupture productive, a precise contrast to the inward rupture that releases fujur.
God grows grain in the opened earth, completing the productive breach of 80:26.
Fruit and pasture extend the crop sequence and connect the opened ground to both people and grazing animals.
The growth is provision for people and their livestock, identifying what the rightly opened and watered earth yields.
Water descends "بِقَدَرٍ," is lodged in earth, and can be taken away; measure, hidden provision, and irreversible loss all bear on the violated drinking share.
The measured stored water produces gardens of palms and grapes, giving the flourishing field made possible by the order in 23:18.
Blessed water descends and grows gardens and harvested grain, directly joining sky-water, worked earth, and crop.
Tall palms with layered clusters display the intact, fruitful palm-head that the source section's secondary ʿaqr sense places under threat.
The crop is provision, and dead land is revived by rain; this states the life-bearing outcome opposite the section's barren field.
Good land brings vegetation abundantly, while bad land produces only scant growth; this is a Quranic two-field contrast closely matching the section's cultivated and buried soul-fields.
A lifeless earth stirs, swells, and grows after rain; the revival is the specific reverse of the field made barren by Thamud's act and punishment.
Each garden gives full produce and God makes a river burst through them, "وَفَجَّرْنَا خِلَالَهُمَا نَهَرًا"; f-j-r here sustains measured fertility.
The flourishing garden may become "صَعِيدًا زَلَقًا," bare slippery ground; this is a direct reversal from cultivated estate to leveled, unproductive land.
Its water may become sunken beyond recovery, showing the withheld-provision side of the water whose measured availability Thamud violated.
The fruit is encompassed and the trellises collapse, making a built and cultivated estate share one destructive consequence.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, linking night-cover with an irreversible field judgment.
By morning the garden is "كَالصَّرِيمِ," stripped or darkened; the ayah meets the section's night, severing, and barren-field images at once.
The garden owners swear they will cut its crop in the morning; this supplies the intended severing whose nocturnal reversal appears in 68:19-20.
They make no exception to their plan, exposing the false confidence that no counter-turn will intervene before the night's judgment.
A rainstorm leaves a thin-soiled rock bare, turning an outwardly fertile surface into sterility; it is the ruined moral field opposite genuine cultivation.
Those seeking God's pleasure are like a high garden whose rain doubles its yield; beside 2:264 it supplies the section's two inward fields and their unlike harvests.
إِنَّ النَّفْسَ لَأَمَّارَةٌ بِالسُّوءِ gives the soul an inward impulse toward evil unless shown mercy, clarifying how the inspired possibilities become a lived direction.
قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ almost restates 91:9, confirming cultivation or purification of the self as the successful field opposed to burial.
Whoever purifies himself "فَإِنَّمَا يَتَزَكَّىٰ لِنَفْسِهِ" and the journey ends with God; the soul both receives the cultivation and bears its outcome.
Those who accept guidance receive more guidance and God "آتَاهُمْ تَقْوَاهُمْ"; this closely echoes the soul being given its taqwa while stressing the guided reception of it.
فَأَمَّا مَن طَغَىٰ begins the moral choice with transgression, linking the creation sequence of 79:27-33 to the same inward disorder as Thamud.
إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لَيَطْغَىٰ locates the overflow in the human being, closely matching the section's movement from cosmic order into inward transgression.
The human transgresses upon seeing himself self-sufficient; this gives the self-launching breach in 96:6 a specific inward cause.
Preferring the nearer life states what the transgressor of 79:37 chooses before the contrasting restraint in 79:40.
One who fears standing before the Lord "وَنَهَى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الْهَوَىٰ" restrains the soul, the clearest nonlexical parallel to taqwa as a dam holding back overflow.
The garden is the refuge of the self-restraining person, completing the cultivated-field outcome opposite transgression.
Giving and "وَاتَّقَىٰ" begin one of two inward courses, closely paralleling the section's paired portions and fields.
God eases the giving, Godfearing person toward ease; the result shows one course of the soul becoming a fitted path.
The miser who deems himself self-sufficient begins the opposite course to 92:5, a specific moral reversal rather than merely another outcome.
God eases that person toward hardship, completing the two-path consequence that the section pictures as two fields.
God guides the human to the way, whether grateful or ungrateful; the two possible responses parallel the soul's given capacities without using the section's field imagery.
وَهَدَيْنَاهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ gives the human two evident ways, a concise parallel to the soul receiving two opposed directions and then choosing.
The fasting ayah calls spouses garments for one another, sets a night-time boundary, and ends "لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَّقُونَ"; covering and restraint thus meet within one legal scene.
Fasting is prescribed "لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ"; bodily abstention makes the restraining sense of taqwa concrete.
The condemned person can only "يَتَّقِي بِوَجْهِهِ" the punishment; this desperate bodily shielding reverses the sound protective cover of taqwa developed in the section.
Pharaoh's people deny signs, so God destroys them "بِذُنُوبِهِمْ" and drowns them; sin, water, and communal consequence meet as they do in the section's Thamud reading.
A former people are destroyed "بِذُنُوبِهِمْ" after being established amid rain and rivers; their sin turns a flourishing water-built settlement into removal.
Earlier peoples were stronger and left greater traces in the earth, yet God seized them "بِذُنُوبِهِمْ"; built landscape and sin's aftermath are explicitly joined.
Like Pharaoh's people and those before them, deniers are seized "بِذُنُوبِهِمْ"; it supports the section's claim that the return follows the deed.
God raises in every community a messenger, then commands the reader to see the deniers' outcome; divine baʿth and communal ʿaqiba meet in one ayah, just as the section joins them around Thamud.
God "بَعَثَ اللَّهُ النَّبِيِّينَ" as bearers of good news and warning; the explicit divine agent supplies the contrast to the unbidden self-rising of 91:12.
God "فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ غُرَابًا" to show Cain what to do; an animal is deliberately sent by God, sharply contrasting the section's man who launches himself like an unhobbling animal.
God takes people by night and "يَبْعَثُكُمْ فِيهِ" by day; daily raising is placed inside the night-day watch that the section transfers into the soul.
God raises the sleepers, "ثُمَّ بَعَثْنَاهُمْ," after their long stillness; the explicit raiser and passive awakening preserve the agency contrast with 91:12.
Retaliation must match what was suffered, using repeated ʿ-q-b forms; the bounded equivalence clarifies the source section's link between what comes after and a measured return.
The garden is "عُقْبَى الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوا" while the unbelievers' outcome is fire; this explicitly joins taqwa to its aftermath, unlike Thamud's ruin.
وَالْعَاقِبَةُ لِلتَّقْوَىٰ compresses the section's two linked terms: restraint determines what follows.
The final home is for those who do not seek elevation or corruption on earth, and "الْعَاقِبَةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ"; it reverses Thamud's proud building and earthly فساد.
The evildoers' "عَاقِبَةَ" is the worst because they deny God's signs; consequence follows denial with the same logic as the Thamud close.
The command to travel and see the criminals' "عَاقِبَةُ" turns ruined places into evidence of the aftermath the section locates in Thamud's houses.
A day comes "لَا مَرَدَّ لَهُ مِنَ اللَّهِ"; the absence of any repelling turn directly illuminates the section's claim that final judgment has no successor to undo it.
The same warning names a day from God for which there is no repelling; it restates the terminal, unreversible turn developed at the section's close.
The promised punishment is declared certain to occur; 52:8 supplies its lack of any repeller, matching the section's finality.
مَا لَهُ مِن دَافِعٍ states directly that nothing can push the punishment away once it comes.
